Part A follows the slides (black) and the doctor's notes (green) — the slides cover the investigation of surgical patients. Part B covers the practical procedures exactly as the gifts asked them (red) — airway, access, lines, chest tube, tubes and catheters, local anaesthesia and sutures.

Part A — Investigation of the surgical patient

Why we investigate before surgery

  • Pre-operative investigations identify conditions that may significantly affect surgical outcomes and recovery, and give anaesthetists and surgeons the information to plan perioperative care.
  • However, 60–70% of routine pre-operative laboratory tests are unnecessary → higher costs, surgical delays, resource inefficiency.
  • Case study (Debre Tabor Hospital, 2023): 350 tests ordered for 247 surgical patients — 20% unnecessary (no guideline justification). Evidence-based protocols would have cut costs without compromising safety.
  • Guiding principles: tests should be selective and purposeful, not routine — driven by the clinical history, physical examination findings and co-morbidity assessment. Routine testing without indication → inefficiency, unnecessary follow-up tests, higher costs, minimal benefit.
  • Pre-operative investigation is not box-ticking: every test answers whether this patient can safely tolerate this operation, and what must be fixed first.
  • Four goals: identify risk factors · assess overall health (including undiagnosed disease) · optimize before operating (glycaemia, BP, anaemia, electrolytes) · improve outcome.
  • Core concept: investigation is the bridge between knowing the patient and operating safely — its output is a modified perioperative plan, not a stack of results.

The general approach

  • History → physical examination → assess & optimize comorbidities → selective investigation.
  • History is the same structured history as any specialty (chief complaint, HPC with onset/aggravating/relieving factors, PMH, family history, medications, allergies, previous anaesthesia, functional status).
  • Rule of thumb: history + examination are the two pillars that direct all further tests. Ordering imaging first and thinking later produces random tests and missed risk factors.
  • A diagnosis is not an assessment — always ask whether the comorbidity is controlled. "Diabetic" is not an assessment; "diabetic with HbA1c 11% and no recent review" is.
ComorbidityWhy it mattersIf left unoptimized
DiabetesPoor control impairs healing and immunity↑ complications, ↑ infection
HypertensionUncontrolled BP destabilises haemodynamics at inductionAnaesthesia may cancel/postpone the case

Pre-operative investigations

  • Common tests: CBC (anaemia, infection risk, platelets), renal function (urea, electrolytes, creatinine), blood glucose (hyperglycaemia ↑ infection, impairs healing), urinalysis (before urologic/invasive surgery — exclude UTI), CXR & ECG (cardiopulmonary risk factors or high-risk surgery).
ConditionIndicated testing (slides)
Healthy, < 40 yearsHaemoglobin; urine pregnancy test if of childbearing potential
Healthy, > 40 yearsAdd ECG and blood glucose
Cardiovascular diseaseECG, CXR, Hb, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
Recent MI, unstable angina, decompensated CHF, significant arrhythmia, severe valve diseaseCardiology consultation
Previous MI, mild stable angina, compensated CHF, diabetesStress test if high-risk surgery or low functional capacity; consider echo
Non-sinus rhythm, abnormal ECG, stroke, advanced age, low functional capacityStress test if high-risk surgery + low functional capacity
Pulmonary diseaseCXR, Hb, glucose, ECG
AsthmaPFT or peak flow
COPDConsider PFT and ABG
Cough / dyspnoeaEvaluate the cause
SmokingStop smoking 4–8 weeks before surgery
MalnutritionTests for the primary disease + albumin and lymphocyte count; severe → consider postponing and supplementing
CategoryContents
LaboratoryCBC · coagulation profile · blood group, screen & crossmatch · renal function · liver function · glucose · electrolytes · urinalysis
Imaging & otherChest X-ray · ECG · targeted CT/MRI when indicated · PFTs · echocardiography
  • Selection is driven by patient factors (disease, symptoms, age, comorbidities, functional status), the type and magnitude of the procedure, and the organ system involved.
  • Coagulation profile matters for three reasons: bleeding risk, DIC, and thrombotic risk.
  • Crossmatch is procedure-specific: minor surgery may need none; major open aortic surgery ≈ 4 units.
  • Glucose may reveal previously undiagnosed diabetes.
  • CT/MRI are for a specific question and are often already done during the diagnostic work-up (don't repeat).
Governing equation: patient risk + procedure risk → need for further testing. Neither axis decides alone.
  • PFTs: justified by pulmonary disease or symptoms (especially chronic cough) plus a physiologically stressful operation (e.g. open aortic surgery). Poor pulmonary reserve → difficult/failed extubation, unplanned ICU admission, prolonged stay, pneumonia.
  • Cardiac testing beyond an ECG (e.g. echo) is decided by the same two axes.

VTE prophylaxis

VTE riskBleeding riskProphylaxis (slides)
Very low—Early ambulation
Low—Mechanical (IPC)
ModerateLowLMWH or LDUH or IPC
ModerateHighIPC
HighLowLMWH or LDUH with IPC
HighHighIPC until bleeding risk falls, then LMWH/LDUH
  • Think about DVT/VTE prophylaxis in every surgical patient — the form depends on risk, but the question is never skipped.
  • Minor surgery, mobile, early discharge → early mobilisation may suffice. Major abdominal/colon surgery with immobility → pharmacological prophylaxis.

The surgical safety checklist

  • WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (19 items): pre-anaesthesia check (identity, procedure, consent, site marking, critical investigations) → pre-incision time-out (team introductions, re-verify patient/procedure, critical steps, anticipated issues) → post-procedure review (procedure done, instrument counts, specimen labelling, recovery concerns). Improves teamwork and communication and reduces surgical errors.

WHO checklist phases

  • A whole-team responsibility (surgery, anaesthesia, nursing), in three phases:
PhaseWhat is confirmed
1 · Pre-anaesthesia checkIdentity · procedure · consent · site marking (critical for paired structures) · important clinical issues
2 · Time-outCollective reconfirmation of patient, procedure, consent, site, antibiotic prophylaxis and critical issues — members actively verify
3 · Post-procedure reviewWhat was done · complications · extra interventions · extubation status · destination (ward vs ICU)
  • Critical issues raised at time-out: severe COPD, severe CAD, expected duration, estimated blood loss, blood availability, anaesthetic plan, expected difficult extubation, ICU need.
  • Example — open aortic reconstruction: consent done, site marked, ≈ 4 h, ≈ 4 L blood loss, 4 units crossmatched, stable CAD, mild COPD, GA ± epidural, ICU if difficult extubation.
  • ★ Professor's emphasis: communication and documentation are among the most commonly missed aspects of surgical care — with clinical and medicolegal consequences. Build good habits early.
  • Quality improvement: identify a deficiency and implement change (e.g. a project to reduce surgical-site infection).

Investigating SSI & preventing wrong-site surgery

  • SSI investigation data points: procedure details, personnel, patient temperature maintenance, bowel preparation, timing and choice of prophylactic antibiotics, skin preparation, operating-room traffic.
  • Wrong-site/wrong-procedure prevention: site marking with indelible ink (with the patient), consistent documentation of images/reports/consent, time-out immediately before incision (patient, procedure, site, implants), clear communication.
  • Root cause analysis: communication failures in ~70% of wrong-site/wrong-procedure errors.
  • Workflow: comprehensive assessment → selective testing → safety protocols (WHO checklist, time-out) → post-op monitoring (SSI surveillance) → quality improvement (audit and feedback).
  • Conclusion: evidence-based selective testing improves outcomes and cuts cost; checklists and infection-investigation tools drive quality; teamwork and communication prevent errors.

Part B — Practical procedures (from past exams)

Airway

  • Unconscious trauma patient, possible C-spine injury, snoring/low saturation → open the airway with a jaw thrust (no head tilt) 438 ×3 432 ×3; maxillofacial fracture → jaw thrust. 432
  • Dyspnoea with severe maxillofacial injury → cricothyroidotomy (surgical airway). 432 ×5
  • Respiratory failure after extubation (accessory muscles, paradoxical breathing, confusion) → reintubate immediately. 439

Vascular access & monitoring

  • Most rapid access in an adult trauma when peripheral IV fails → intraosseous. 432 ×2
  • Venous cut-down site → great saphenous vein anterior to the medial malleolus 437 Final ×9 436 ×2 427
  • Beat-to-beat (real-time) BP → arterial line in the radial artery 437 Final ×2; if the radial can't be used → brachial artery. 439

Central venous catheter

  • Indications: TPN/feeding, rapid fluid and blood administration, vein-irritant drugs, CVP monitoring, no peripheral access. Sites: internal jugular, subclavian, femoral (or a peripheral vein in the antecubital fossa = PICC).
  • Not an indication → "all abdominal surgery". 437; sites → IJV (and subclavian; EJV is a peripheral vein). 435
  • Subclavian insertion position → head down (Trendelenburg) — distends the vein and prevents air embolism. 436 ×2
  • Correct tip position on CXR → at the level of the carina (lower SVC, T4/5) 437 ×4 437 Final ×5 Final
  • After subclavian insertion → chest X-ray (tip position + pneumothorax). 429 Final ×2 427
  • Hypotension, tachycardia and desaturation 2 h after a subclavian line → tension pneumothorax 438 ×3; keyed "most common" complication → tension pneumothorax 437; least common → myocarditis 437; convulsion is not a complication. 426
  • TPN line with fever and S. aureus bacteraemia → remove the catheter, culture the tip. 438 ×8

Chest tube & needle decompression

  • Needle decompression of tension pneumothorax → 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line (ATLS 10 now prefers 4th–5th ICS mid-axillary in adults) 436 ×4; ventilated trauma patient, hard to bag, ↓ air entry on the left → needle decompression, left 2nd ICS. 430
  • Chest tube site = "safe triangle": 4th/5th intercostal space, anterior-to-mid-axillary line (nipple level in men) — keyed: 4th ICS above the 5th rib mid-axillary 437 ×2 439 Final ×2; mid-axillary 5th 428 Final ×2 427; one version keyed mid-axillary 6th 429 Final; quick landmark → level of the nipple. 435
  • Chest tube is done with full aseptic technique 436; confirming with CT is irrelevant (CXR after insertion) 438; pneumoperitoneum is not an indication (pneumothorax, haemothorax, chylothorax, empyema are). 437

Nasogastric tube

  • Indications: decompression in ileus/obstruction, GI bleeding (lavage/assessment), feeding, drug administration, perforated viscus (to reduce contamination) — keyed differently by year (see below).
  • Contraindication to the nasal route: base-of-skull fracture (and severe maxillofacial injury) → use the oral route.
  • Avoid the nasal route in head injury with skull-base fracture. 429 Final
  • Confirm placement by aspirating gastric contents (pH) 438 435; another version keyed auscultation (air insufflation) — X-ray is the most reliable. 436
  • Indication → GI bleeding 436; perforated duodenal ulcer keyed as an indication in one year 436 and as not an indication in another (vs ileus, obstruction, GI bleed). 438 Final

Urinary catheters

  • Foley insertion → lubricate the catheter tip (aseptic technique, usually 14–16 Fr, no anaesthesia needed). 438 ×2
  • Suprapubic catheter: insert two fingers (4–5 cm) above the symphysis pubis 437; used for urethral stricture/injury and bladder-neck obstruction — not for ureteric stricture 437; complications: infection, pelvic-vessel and bowel injury — not liver injury. 437
  • Retention after hernia repair despite two in-out catheterizations → Foley with trial of void in a few days. 437 ×2

Local anaesthesia, spinal & epidural

  • Earliest sign of local-anaesthetic toxicity → perioral numbness (then tinnitus, confusion, seizures, arrhythmia). 437 ×4
  • Longest-acting local anaesthetic → bupivacaine. 435
  • Contraindicated: lidocaine with adrenaline in an ingrowing-toenail (digital) block → ischaemia. 429
  • Inguinal hernia repair under local → block the ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves (keyed iliohypogastric). 429
  • Lumbar puncture landmark → line joining the iliac crests (L4) — below the end of the cord 438 Final ×4; keyed "posterior superior iliac crest" in 432. 432 Final
  • Post-dural-puncture headache: initial bed rest, fluids, analgesics — blood patch is not initial 438; definitive/last → epidural blood patch. 435

Sutures & wounds

  • Skin closure after a superficial forearm lipoma → 4-0 Monocryl, cutting needle, subcuticular 438 ×4; 7-cm back lipoma → keyed monofilament non-absorbable subcuticular. 438
  • Face sutures out at 3–5 days: keyed 4 days 438, "at least 2 days" 436, day 5. 435
  • Clean forehead laceration → primary closure 436 Final; puncture wound → leave open, oral antibiotics. 436 Final

FAST & diagnostic peritoneal lavage

  • FAST examines 4 areas: pericardial, RUQ (Morison's), LUQ (splenorenal), pelvis 432 ×4; it can't see the pancreas 439 ×2 or retroperitoneal haemorrhage (eFAST adds the chest for pneumothorax/haemothorax). 431
  • DPL absolute contraindication → an existing indication for laparotomy (expanding abdomen after a stab wound) 431; DPL "all true except" → keyed "indicated in unexplained shock" (NGT, Foley and an infra-umbilical incision are part of it). 427

Other

  • Anaphylaxis to IV contrast (urticaria, wheeze) → epinephrine 436 ×9 426
  • Universal precautions: never re-sheath needles (use a sharps container). 438
  • Antiemetic → ondansetron 435; ERCP can't be done after gastrectomy (no access to the papilla, e.g. Billroth II/Roux-en-Y). 426
